title: Quick check: Pretraining Large Models

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes defining a pretraining objective in the context of pretraining large models?
options: For defining a pretraining objective, distinguish the training objective from the evaluation goal. Check provenance and data quality, keep validation/test examples isolated from training, record the baseline and configuration, and evaluate both improvement on the target task and possible regressions elsewhere.
A fluent result is enough to establish correctness, so the input and assumptions do not need checking.
The concept can be implemented entirely in a prompt; application validation and testing are unnecessary.
Use the largest available model for every task and skip a baseline or documented acceptance criteria.
questions.answer_key: For defining a pretraining objective, distinguish the training objective from the evaluation goal. Check provenance and data quality, keep validation/test examples isolated from training, record the baseline and configuration, and evaluate both improvement on the target task and possible regressions elsewhere.
questions.explanation: For defining a pretraining objective, distinguish the training objective from the evaluation goal. Check provenance and data quality, keep validation/test examples isolated from training, record the baseline and configuration, and evaluate both improvement on the target task and possible regressions elsewhere. This is why the lesson treats the concept as something to apply and verify, not as a guarantee of quality.

questions.prompt: Which practice gives the clearest evidence that constructing large-scale training datasets is working in pretraining large models?
options: Test only one easy input, then assume the behavior generalizes to every language, user, and data source.
Skip validation because a well-formatted answer implies the model followed the intended process.
Change the prompt, model, data, and settings at the same time, then attribute any difference to one cause.
Use representative cases, an explicit success criterion, and retained failure examples; compare results against a baseline before relying on the behavior.
questions.answer_key: Use representative cases, an explicit success criterion, and retained failure examples; compare results against a baseline before relying on the behavior.
questions.explanation: Constructing large-scale training datasets should be evaluated with evidence appropriate to its use. Representative tests and a baseline help reveal failures and avoid overstating what the example proves.

questions.prompt: A team applies defining a pretraining objective from pretraining large models and gets a plausible result, but it has not checked an edge case. What should it do next?
options: Remove guardrails or access checks to make the next run more likely to succeed.
Increase model size and deploy immediately, without retaining a baseline or regression tests.
Reproduce the case with controlled input, check source/evidence and intermediate steps where available, test an edge case, and document remaining uncertainty.
Accept the result because confidence and fluency are reliable substitutes for measurement.
questions.answer_key: Reproduce the case with controlled input, check source/evidence and intermediate steps where available, test an edge case, and document remaining uncertainty.
questions.explanation: A plausible answer is not proof. Controlled tests, evidence checks, and explicit uncertainty help identify incorrect assumptions and unsafe failure modes.
